item.title: AP's refusal to give Trump rights to Butler photo helped fuel Oval Office ban, report claims
item.description: Trump's administration targeted the Associated Press over photo rights to Evan Vucci's iconic Butler, Pennsylvania, assassination attempt image, according to a NYT report.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump's administration targeted the Associated Press (AP) over rights to the iconic photo of the president in Butler, Pennsylvania, taken after an assassination attempt, according to a New York Times report.

The AP has repeatedly sparred with the Trump White House after the president was elected in 2024. 

The outlet was banned from the Oval Office and Air Force One shortly after Trump was inaugurated because the AP continued to use "Gulf of Mexico" after the president renamed it the Gulf of America in 2025. The ban has led to a First Amendment battle in court.

However, according to the Times, White House aides also connected the ban to the AP's refusal to give them rights to the infamous photo of the president after he was shot. The Times cited two people briefed on a private lunch with Trump and network anchors in 2025.

INSIDE AP’S FIRST AMENDMENT BATTLE WITH TRUMP’S WHITE HOUSE AS ‘GULF OF AMERICA’ DISPUTE HEADS BACK TO COURT

"We’re focused on continuing to stand for the right of the public and the press to speak freely without government retaliation or control," a spokesman for the AP told Fox News Digital in a statement in response to the claim. 

A source added the White House has not communicated this reasoning to the AP.

The White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Trump was rushed offstage by Secret Service agents after gunfire grazed his upper right ear during his July 13, 2024, rally in Butler, Pennsylvania. The attack came months before Trump’s re-election and preceded a series of later alleged attempts and reported threats against his life.

The president was mid-sentence, pointing to a chart on illegal immigration under the Biden administration, when gunshots pierced the air at his Butler rally. Authorities identified the gunman as Thomas Matthew Crooks, who fired from the roof of a nearby building.

TWO MEN SHOT AT TRUMP'S BUTLER RALLY SUE FEDERAL GOVERNMENT OVER SECRET SERVICE 'PREVENTABLE FAILURES'

Secret Service agents tackled Trump to the ground. Moments later, as they rose to escort him to his motorcade, Trump emerged from the huddle. Trump raised his fist high in the air, and said "fight" three times, prompting the audience to erupt and chant "U-S-A!" as he exited.

The gunman killed firefighter Corey Comperatore, who was shielding his family, and wounded two other men. A Secret Service sniper killed Crooks during the attack.

A photo of Trump, captured by Evan Vucci of the AP, with his fist raised and blood visible on his face, quickly went viral and landed on the front pages of newspapers across the world.

"I was literally just thinking about doing the best possible job I could, because I knew that this was a moment in American history that I had to be at the top of my game for," Vucci told Fox News Digital in July 2024, after the assassination attempt.

TRUMP SIGNS PROCLAMATION DECLARING FEBRUARY 9 'GULF OF AMERICA DAY' AHEAD OF SUPER BOWL: 'ANOTHER BIG WIN'

"I knew immediately it was gunfire. I trained my lens on the stage, and I saw Secret Service agents going to run to the president, covering him up. And from that moment, I ran to the stage and I got my wide angle lens, and I started making photographs. I went into work mode," Vucci said. "I knew immediately that it was going to be one of the most important things I'll ever photograph, and that I needed to do the best job possible."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Vucci switched to a wide angle to ensure the flag flying above got in his shot. He noticed an SUV parked at the side of the stage as Secret Service agents covered Trump and chaos erupted around him. Vucci said he "sprinted" to the side of the stage, assuming it was where Trump would exit, and got in position to snap photos as Trump pumped his fist toward the crowd.

"That’s where I was when he was coming down… and that's the photo a lot of people are sharing," he said.

item.title: Lindsay Clancy juror says panel saw case as chance to 'make it better for other women'

item.content:encoded:
One of the 11 jurors who wanted to find Massachusetts mom Lindsay Clancy not criminally responsible for killing her three children said the panel viewed the case as a chance to make things "better for other women" and families — a thought process that one legal analyst is calling "problematic."

"Even though we didn't know what was going on outside of our little bubble that we were in, we knew that this was a turning point, and this would be something that could change something to make it better for other women in the future, for other families," 65-year-old Clancy juror Paula Devlin told "CBS Saturday Morning" over the weekend. Several jurors and Clancy's defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, have claimed that the holdout at the end didn't show his fellow jurors the evidence that he believed pointed toward guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

item.title: Florida State fires AD Michael Alford, as Mike Norvell’s seat reaches a boiling point in Tallahassee
item.description: The Florida State board of trustees ousted Michael Alford with an Alabama game looming that could seal Mike Norvell's fate in Tallahassee soon.
item.content:encoded:
Following a tumultuous two seasons for the Florida State football program, the school fired atheltic director Michael Alford on Monday morning.

The decision comes after another lackluster performance from the Seminoles against SMU last week, that also saw the lights go out inside the stadium that should have been seen as a sign of things to come in Tallahassee.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL’S CHAOS ERA IS HERE: TEXAS RALLIES, OREGON FALLS AND LANE KIFFIN EYES RETURN TO OLE MISS

There have been multiple conversations over the past few weeks regarding the status of Alford, who has been at the forefront of concerns about the direction of the Seminoles athletic department, with fundraising being a major point of concern for officials in this current era of college athletics.

Since the 2023 season, FSU fans have witnessed the football program go 8-13, with the crowd inside Doak Campbell Stadium loudly voicing their displeasure with head coach Mike Norvell.

But, the questions loomed as to what, and who, would be making the decision on the future direction of the football program.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL COACHES ON HOT SEAT: BILL BELICHICK, MIKE NORVELL AND OTHERS FACING MAKE-OR-BREAK 2026

Now, with Michael Alford being fired, and associate AD Bruce Warwick taking over in the interim, it's clear that the Florida State board of trustees are planning to make further moves.

Even though Alford did not hire Norvell at Florida State, decisions made during his tenure have had a major impact on the Seminoles future.

One of the moves made during his tenure as AD came when Alford helped put together the fundraising for a new $380 million upgrade to Doak Campbell Stadium, while the school has been mid-pack when it comes to a revenue-sharing budget to field a football team.

Currently sitting at 39-35, Norvell is currently sitting on the hottest seat in college football. His record of 8-18 since the infamous 2023 season has left boosters involved with the Florida State athletic department befuddled, also knowing it will cost them upwards of $50 million to fire Norvell if that decision is made.

FROM POWER FAILURES TO MORAL VICTORIES, MONDAY NIGHT COULDN'T HAVE GONE MUCH WORSE FOR FLORIDA STATE FANS

Monday morning, Florida State Board of Trustees chairman Peter Collins released the following statement on the firing of Alford.

"We have made significant investments and structural changes in our athletics program and Seminole Boosters over the past few years, but more are needed. This step begins the next phase of restructuring that the University must commit to in order to compete in this era of college sports.  The President and the Board are in lockstep on the mission and what the results must be."

If you remember, Florida State also sued its own conference (ACC) in 2023 over the binding grant of rights contract, which led to the the league lowering the buyout for member schools, with a full buyout of $75 million being in place following the 2029-2030 year.

Were the Seminoles looking for an exit to the Big Ten or SEC? Sure, but if they are planning to garner a significant payday in a future move, the school needs to get its affairs in order.

KEEP AN EYE ON THESE UNDER-THE-RADAR NAMES DURING THIS SEASON'S COLLEGE FOOTBALL COACHING CAROUSEL

And, that starts with the football program.

Right now, the Seminoles have lost enough ground to other major brands around college football that getting back near the top will be a task in of its own.

An upcoming game against Alabama this weekend could be the final nail in the coffin for Norvell, which already feels like a foregone conclusion among many within the athletic department.

Would the school wait until a new athletic director is hired before moving on from Norvell if he cannot pull off a miracle over the next two months?

FSU-SMU GAME TURNS INTO OLD-SCHOOL FOOTBALL AFTER STADIUM POWER OUTAGE WIPES OUT IN-GAME COMMUNICATION

Many within the FSU community don't know if he even gets to November at this point.

The first move in making a change of this magnitude is installing the next athletic director to make decisions regarding future hires, or firings.

Florida State took care of the first part on Monday with Michael Alford. Now, we wait to see how long Mike Norvell lasts in Tallahassee if these results keep piling up.

The latest shakeup in college athletics is a big one, and FSU was clearly not waiting around for it to get worse.

item.title: Libertarian tech mogul to hit DSA with an eight-figure spending nuke
